name: Cucumber extract
lead: Cucumber extract is a preparation made from the fruit, and sometimes the seeds, of Cucumis sativus, an annual vine of the gourd family that has been cultivated for at least 3,000 years [1]. In skincare it is listed as a cooling, soothing botanical and is found in cleansers, toners, gels, sheet masks and eye products, where it is used for its fresh feel and mild, hydrating character.

People use it to look more rested and refreshed. The image of cucumber slices over closed eyes is a long-standing beauty ritual aimed at puffy, tired-looking eyes, and cucumber-based products carry that association into daily routines. The raw fruit is about 95 percent water, which is the basis of its reputation as a hydrating, cooling ingredient [1].

Research labelled "cucumber extract" covers several different subjects: many indexed papers concern sea cucumbers, which are marine animals unrelated to the garden cucumber, and several use cucumber extract as a laboratory reagent [2][3][21]. For the garden cucumber, published work includes a standardized aqueous extract assessed for oral safety [4], an iminosugar compound isolated from the fruit that reduced inflammatory activity in laboratory assays [5], and a placebo-controlled trial in knee osteoarthritis [6]. A small trial of cucumber seed extract for sun-induced redness is registered [7].

paras: Cucumber is botanically a pepo, a type of berry, though it is treated as a vegetable in cooking. Slicing, pickling and seedless types are the main groups [1]. The raw fruit with peel is mostly water with small amounts of carbohydrate and protein (about 16 kcal per 100 g) and notable vitamin K, and polyphenol content is higher in unpeeled fruit [1]. The fresh aroma includes a compound called cucumber aldehyde, and cucurbitacins give the rind a slightly bitter taste in some varieties [1].

Cosmetic extracts may be made from the juice, the fruit pulp or the seeds. A branded standardized aqueous cucumber extract, sold as a nutraceutical ingredient, has been the subject of published safety and osteoarthritis work [4][6].

Beyond water, the fruit contains small amounts of carbohydrate and protein, vitamin K and polyphenols, with more polyphenol in the unpeeled fruit [1]. Wild and some cultivated cucurbits make cucurbitacins, bitter triterpene compounds that act as a defence against herbivores; in cucumber, a 2014 Science study identified nine genes in the biosynthesis pathway and showed that a recessive allele selected during domestication makes cultivated fruit non-bitter [22]. Eating foods very high in cucurbitacins can cause illness known as toxic squash syndrome, which is why bitterness is a warning sign in cucurbits [22].

A distinct compound of research interest is idoBR1, an iminosugar amino acid isolated in 2020 from certain cucumbers. In laboratory assays it reduced lipopolysaccharide-induced tumor necrosis factor alpha in a human monocyte cell line and in ex vivo human blood, inhibited some sialidase and iduronidase enzymes, and reduced hyaluronic acid binding to the cell receptor CD44; the authors proposed that it acts by inhibiting an induced sialidase, and noted it is excreted unchanged in urine after consumption [5]. The standardized extract Q-Actin is standardized to roughly 1 to 2 percent of this compound [4].

The cucumber originated in Asia across a region from India to southern China and northern Thailand, and was domesticated in India from a wild relative [1]. Records show it reaching France by the 9th century, England by the 14th and North America by the mid-16th century, and the Roman emperor Tiberius is reported to have eaten it year-round [1]. Wikipedia's account of the plant does not mention cosmetic use; the slices-on-the-eyes image is part of popular beauty culture rather than a documented clinical practice.

Cucumber slices on the eyes are a long-standing popular beauty image, and the extract appears in products marketed to soothe, cool or refresh skin. Manufacturers generally describe its role as soothing and hydrating. Puffy lower lids are described by Wikipedia as almost always due to fluid build-up around the eyes, with causes including ageing, allergy, salt intake, sleep loss and lying flat; it lists head elevation and cold compresses as short-term measures, the latter because cold narrows blood vessels and limits fluid entering the tissue, and it does not mention cucumber [23]. Wikipedia's article on periorbital dark circles lists anatomy, allergies, fatigue, ageing and pigmentation as contributors and mentions caffeine and vitamin C eye creams, also without cucumber [24]. No controlled study of cucumber extract on puffiness, dark circles, redness or other appearance outcomes was found.

Cucumber is best known as a product ingredient and a spa image rather than a looksmaxxing protocol. In looksmaxxing and fitness discussion it appears mainly as a minor ingredient in basic skincare routines; on the T Nation forum, a member looking for ways to drink more water mentions adding a few cucumber slices as a flavouring, a food use rather than a skincare one [8].

Sea cucumber extracts are a separate product family. Wikipedia describes sea cucumbers as marine animals in the class Holothuroidea, related to starfish rather than to the garden cucumber, eaten in Asian cuisines and made into traditional oils, creams and cosmetics such as the Malay remedy gamat [21].

Cucumbers have long been described anecdotally as anti-inflammatory and cooling. Laboratory work on idoBR1 [5] and a clinical study of the standardized extract in knee osteoarthritis [6] are the main published pharmacological findings, and both concern the isolated compound or oral extract rather than topical cucumber preparations.

A single oral dose of the standardized extract was tolerated at 2000 mg/kg in rats, and repeat dosing up to 1000 mg/kg per day for up to 90 days was well tolerated, with mutagenicity testing also reported [4]. These studies concern ingestion and do not directly address topical use. As with other plant extracts, individual allergic or irritant reactions to fragrance or preservative components in finished products are possible.

No published clinical trial has tested cucumber extract for a cosmetic outcome. A 180-day placebo-controlled study of the standardized extract enrolled 101 adults with knee osteoarthritis, 91 of whom completed it, and tested two doses; its authors reported improvements in parameters linked to moderate osteoarthritis [6]. Registered trials include cucumber extract for joint pain (80 participants) [9], a cucumber supplement for arthrosis pain (60 participants) [10], and cucumber seed extract versus placebo for sun-induced skin redness (minimal erythema dose) in 29 adults with Fitzpatrick skin types III to V, listed as completed [7]. Results of these registrations have not been published. Studies of sea cucumber extracts, including several in cancer models and one in a rat liver injury model, concern a different organism and are not evidence about the garden cucumber [2].

The cucumber-on-the-eyes image appears widely in spa and beauty imagery as shorthand for relaxation and a rested look, and cucumber is a common label ingredient in products sold as refreshing or soothing. Cultivation spread from India across Asia and reached Europe and North America over centuries [1]. Cucurbitacin-driven bitterness remains the reason cultivars are selected for mildness [22].

lore.intro: Cucumber's beauty reputation comes mostly from popular culture rather than forums; on the forum material reviewed it appears mainly as a food or flavouring [8].

claims.claim: Cucumber slices on the eyes reduce puffiness and tired looks
claims.believers: Popular beauty culture holds that cool cucumber slices refresh puffy eyes, and many eye products use this association.
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists cold compresses and head elevation as short-term measures for puffy eyes and does not mention cucumber [23]; no controlled study of cucumber on puffiness was found.

claims.claim: Cucumber extract hydrates and soothes skin
claims.believers: Manufacturers describe it as a cooling, hydrating ingredient, pointing to the fruit's roughly 95 percent water content.
claims.experts: The fruit is about 95 percent water [1]; no published trial tests topical cucumber extract for hydration or soothing.

claims.believers: Traditional and wellness sources describe cucumber as anti-inflammatory.
claims.experts: Laboratory assays found the isolated compound idoBR1 reduced inflammatory signalling [5], and a placebo-controlled study of the standardized oral extract reported improved pain-related parameters in knee osteoarthritis [6].

claims.claim: Cucumber extract can reduce sun-induced redness
claims.believers: Some manufacturers position seed extracts as photoprotective.
claims.experts: A cucumber seed extract versus placebo trial using minimal erythema dose in 29 adults is registered as completed; results are not published [7].

claims.claim: Sea cucumber extracts are cucumber extracts
claims.believers: Product listings and some search results use "cucumber extract" for both.
claims.experts: Sea cucumbers are marine animals unrelated to the garden cucumber, so findings about one do not apply to the other [21].

card.summary: A cooling, hydrating botanical in cleansers and eye products; popular imagery, but no controlled evidence for appearance benefits.
card.aka: Cucumis sativus extract, cucumber fruit or seed extract
card.note: Many "cucumber extract" papers are about sea cucumbers, a different organism.

quick.overview:
Cucumber extract is made from the fruit or seeds of the cucumber plant and appears in gels, toners and eye products as a cooling, soothing ingredient.
Its reputation rests largely on the fruit being mostly water and on the familiar image of cucumber slices on the eyes. Published research on skin outcomes is essentially absent.
quick.mechanism: Manufacturers describe it as hydrating and soothing. No studies have measured a specific mechanism on human skin.
quick.risks: Oral toxicity and mutagenicity studies of a standardized extract exist, but they concern ingestion. Topical risks are those of any plant-based cosmetic, mainly individual irritation or allergy to the finished product.

chain: Cooling, water-rich extract applied in gels, toners and eye products
Soothing, hydrating feel on the skin
Fresher, calmer-looking skin and eye area
angle.text: People apply cucumber extract in cleansers, toners and eye products, or place cucumber slices on the eyes, to cool and refresh the skin around them. It is used for a calm, hydrated look rather than for a specific corrective effect.
